query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultrathin refractory interlayer coating on the tungsten surfaces in a W–Cu composite will suppress phase separation and interfacial void formation under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions, thereby improving thermal conductivity compared to the untreated composite.
generation.material_initial_state: W–Cu composite with tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments embedded in a copper matrix that is prone to phase separation and interfacial void formation under service conditions.
generation.intervention: Deposit an ultrathin refractory interlayer coating on all tungsten surfaces prior to composite fabrication, for example via physical vapor deposition.
generation.conditions: During processing, the coating is applied uniformly on W surfaces. In service, the composite is subjected to high thermal flux and irradiation as experienced at joints between W-based plasma-facing components and Cu-based cooling elements.
generation.structural_mediator: An engineered interfacial layer that creates a graded transition between tungsten and copper.
generation.mechanism: The refractory interlayer reduces the interfacial energy mismatch between W and Cu, which in turn suppresses both phase separation and the nucleation of interfacial voids under thermal and irradiation stress. This enhanced bonding prevents defect formation that would otherwise decrease thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated composite will show a marked reduction in phase separation and void formation, leading to improved thermal conductivity relative to the untreated material under the combined stresses of high heat flux and irradiation.
generation.baseline: Untreated W–Cu composites are known to develop phase separation and interfacial voids under service conditions, which degrade thermal conductivity.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable when a uniform, ultrathin refractory coating can be reliably deposited on tungsten surfaces. Its effectiveness is expected under current plasma-facing and cooling component operating conditions; however, performance at temperatures or irradiation levels far beyond current benchmarks remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The ideal coating thickness and its exact refractory composition for optimal performance under the specified extreme conditions need further optimization. Uncertainties also remain about the long-term adhesion and stability of the interlayer under continuous thermal and irradiation cycling.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite specimens: one set with the ultrathin refractory interlayer coating deposited on tungsten surfaces (via PVD) and a control set without the coating. Expose both sets to cyclic heat-transfer and irradiation conditions that simulate operational environments. Post-exposure, perform detailed microstructural analysis to assess phase separation and void formation, and measure thermal conductivity.
measurements: Thermal conductivity (via laser flash analysis or equivalent)
Microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM for interfacial voids and phase identification)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens do not show a statistically significant improvement in thermal conductivity and exhibit similar levels of phase separation and interfacial void formation compared to the untreated controls under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

AbstractIn this study, an effective way of applying Ti/Ni deposited coating to the surface of diamond single crystal particles by magnetron sputtering was proposed and novel high-entropy alloy (HEA)/diamond composites were prepared by spark plasma sintering (SPS). The results show that the interfacial bonding state of the coated diamond composite is obviously better than that of the uncoated diamond composite. Corresponding mechanical properties such as hardness, density, transverse fracture strength and friction properties of the coated diamond composite were also found to be better than those of the uncoated diamond composite. The effects of interface structure and defects on the mechanical properties of HEA/diamond composites were investigated. The research directions for further improving the structure and properties of high-entropy alloy/diamond composites were proposed. Keywords: high-entropy alloy, diamond, coating, interface, mechanical properties

decision.trend: Earlier research in composite systems with challenging interfacial phenomena has increasingly focused on engineering the interface to improve bonding and suppress deleterious effects. For instance, studies such as the Ti/Ni coating on diamond particles (PMC7514646) have demonstrated that a tailored interfacial layer can markedly improve the adhesion between phases. Similarly, first‐principles studies (PMC10608501) have examined the atomic bonding at engineered interfaces while processing studies (PMC10056590) have highlighted the role of interface microstructure control via heat treatments. The overall progression has been from untreated, composition‐controlled systems toward deliberate surface/interfacial modification, but under extreme thermal or irradiation environments some interfaces still suffer from phase separation and void formation.
decision.unsolved: In the specific case of W–Cu composites, phase separation and interfacial void formation under service conditions remain unresolved. Although prior work in other composite systems shows that interface coatings can improve bonding and mitigate defects, the optimal intervention for the W–Cu system—particularly under combined heat-transfer and irradiation conditions—has yet to be demonstrated.
decision.lever: Apply an ultrathin, refractory interlayer coating (e.g., deposited via physical vapor deposition) on the tungsten surfaces prior to composite fabrication
decision.why: This lever logically follows the established trend toward interface engineering that improves phase stability and bonding. An ultrathin refractory layer can serve as a graded transition between W and Cu, reducing interfacial energy mismatch and thereby suppressing phase separation and void nucleation under high thermal flux and irradiation, while preserving or even enhancing thermal conductivity.
